title: Considering Sound in Planning and Designing Public Spaces: A Review of Theory and Applications and a Proposed Framework for Integrating Research and Practice
authors: Bild, E., Coler, M., Pfeffer, K., & Bertolini, L., 2016
central_proposition: This paper proposes an activity-centered framework to integrate diverse scientific and professional knowledge about sound and auditory environments into public space planning and design, by focusing on user activities.

concept_definitions.name: acoustic environment
concept_definitions.definition: characterizations of sounds and the environment relying first on physical measurements with a device

concept_definitions.name: auditory environment
concept_definitions.definition: characterization of sounds and the environment relying first on descriptions of the human experience and afterward related to physical measurements

concept_definitions.name: soundscape
concept_definitions.definition: the acoustic environment as perceived or experienced and/or understood by a person or people, in context

concept_definitions.name: noise
concept_definitions.definition: a term used in policy and research as well as in everyday discourses of users of urban and rural spaces to refer to sounds considered or perceived as unwanted

concept_definitions.name: appropriation
concept_definitions.definition: the interactive process through which humans take over their physical settings, through different means in order to make these spaces their own

argument_structure: The paper reviews existing literature on sound research (object-centered vs. human-centered), sound-related policies (ENM vs. SSD), and technologies. It identifies three gaps in current practice regarding the integration of user activities, the perception of sound as a resource, and the reliance on reductionist acoustic measurements. To address these gaps, it proposes an activity-centered framework that emphasizes the two-way relationship between users, their activities, and their auditory environments, mediated by user characteristics and contextual factors.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The proposed framework posits a two-way causal relationship: users' auditory environments (physical and perceptual features) influence the activities users perform, and conversely, the activities users perform affect their auditory environments. This relationship is modulated by user characteristics (demographics, familiarity, needs, expectations, purpose) and contextual factors (environmental conditions, spatiotemporal aspects, amenities). Integrating these variables through an activity-centered lens allows for a more holistic understanding and design of public spaces that are suitable for intended activities and user needs, moving beyond a 'sound-as-waste' paradigm.

findings.antecedent: vision-oriented approach in urban planning and design
findings.consequent: neglect of multisensory aspects (e.g., sound, smell) in urban experience
findings.mechanism: The dominance of vision in planning practice leads to other senses being considered as an afterthought, resulting in an incomplete understanding of urban experience.
findings.quote: professionals remain mostly anchored in a primarily visual tradition
findings.empirical_support_cited: Montagu 1971; Tuan 1977; Holl, Pallasmaa, and Péréz-Gómez 1994; Lynch, Banerjee, and Southworth 1995; Pallasmaa 2005; Zardini 2005; Porteous 2013

findings.antecedent: sound (as perceived and understood by individuals/society)
findings.consequent: human relationship to community, social relationships, space, and place
findings.mechanism: Sound, particularly as part of a 'soundscape,' is intimately intertwined with how humans experience and relate to their social and physical environments, shaping their sense of belonging and interaction.
findings.quote: Anthropologists, historians, and soundscape researchers depict an intimate relationship between sound and the ways humans relate to community, to social relationships, and to space and place

findings.consequent: negative effects on well-being of urban space users
findings.mechanism: High sound levels are often perceived as 'noise' and can cause annoyance, stress, and other health issues, leading to a focus on sound as a public nuisance in policy.
findings.quote: increasing body of research on the negative effects of sounds that are over particular levels on the well-being of urban space users
findings.empirical_support_cited: World Health Organization [WHO] 2000; Öhrström et al. 2006

findings.antecedent: object-centered approach to sound research (physical measurements)
findings.consequent: knowledge on physical attributes of sounds (e.g., annoyance from traffic noise, health effects)
findings.mechanism: This approach focuses on quantifiable physical properties of sound, leading to insights into how these properties correlate with human responses like annoyance or physiological health impacts.
findings.quote: Object-centered studies produce knowledge on the physical attributes of sounds that, for instance, affect the level of annoyance caused by traffic noise
findings.empirical_support_cited: Lercher 1996; Fujii, Atagi, and Ando 2002; Ising and Kruppa 2004; Babisch 2008

findings.antecedent: human-centered approach to sound research (experiential descriptions)
findings.consequent: understanding of how sounds are perceived, interpreted, and judged by humans (beyond physical properties)
findings.mechanism: By focusing on human experience, this approach reveals that sound perception is not merely signal processing but involves individual and shared knowledge, experience, and expectations, leading to a more nuanced understanding of auditory environments.
findings.quote: sound is not reducible only to a quantifiable 'signal'... the human is at the center of the relationship between humans and sounds
findings.empirical_support_cited: Truax 1995; Guastavino 2007; Dubois, Coler, and Wörtche 2014

findings.antecedent: Environmental Noise Management (ENM) strategy (sound as waste)
findings.consequent: focus on managing and controlling outdoor noise to protect users from deleterious effects
findings.mechanism: Rooted in environmental impact studies and concerns about well-being from noise, ENM aims to reduce unwanted sounds through regulations, zoning, traffic management, and physical alterations, treating sound primarily as a problem to be mitigated.
findings.quote: ENM focuses on sound as a waste that must be managed to protect users of spaces from its deleterious effects.

findings.consequent: focus on purposeful design and improvement of users' auditory environments for pleasantness and enjoyment
findings.mechanism: SSD integrates both physical and perceptual components of sound, incorporating user experience and expectations to design auditory environments that are perceived as pleasant, often through participatory planning and active/passive measures.
findings.quote: SSD addresses sound as a resource and thus focuses on the purposeful design and improvement of users' auditory environments for it to be perceived as pleasant to and enjoyable by users

findings.consequent: users' perception and evaluation of auditory environments
findings.mechanism: The specific activities users perform (e.g., resting, socializing, working) influence how they perceive and evaluate the sounds and overall auditory environment, determining whether it is considered appropriate or restorative.
findings.quote: the evaluation and description of sounds and auditory environments may vary according to the activities that users perform
findings.empirical_support_cited: Nielbo 2015; Bild et al. 2015; Steffens, Steele, and Guastavino 2015

findings.antecedent: users' characteristics (demographics, familiarity, needs, expectations, purpose)
findings.consequent: users' perception and evaluation of auditory environments
findings.mechanism: Individual and collective characteristics of users (e.g., age, gender, cultural background, prior experience) shape their auditory expectations and sensitivities, leading to differential perceptions and evaluations of soundscapes.
findings.quote: Psychological studies are also sensitive to the diversity of users, accounting for intragroup differences and user characteristics
findings.empirical_support_cited: Yu and Kang 2008; Booi and van der Berg 2012; Nielbo, Steele, and Guastavino 2013

findings.antecedent: users' auditory environments (physical and perceptual features)
findings.consequent: activities users perform in public spaces
findings.mechanism: The qualities of the auditory environment can enable or discourage certain activities, influencing how users choose to engage with and appropriate a public space.
findings.quote: research indicates that users' auditory environments in public spaces are perceived as enabling or discouraging certain categories of activities
findings.empirical_support_cited: Nielbo, Steele, and Guastavino 2013; Steffens, Steele, and Guastavino 2015; Nielbo 2015

findings.consequent: auditory environments (transformation of suitability for other users)
findings.mechanism: Users are not just passive receivers but active producers of sound. Their activities generate sounds that can alter the auditory environment, making it more or less suitable for other users' purposes, needs, and expectations.
findings.quote: the activities that users perform affect their auditory environments and transform it in ways that other users may find suitable or not for their purpose

findings.antecedent: reliance on reductionist acoustic measurements and technologies in planning practice
findings.consequent: limited incorporation of user knowledge and activities in urban planning and design
findings.mechanism: Current planning practices prioritize easily quantifiable acoustic data and technologies, which often fail to capture the complex, subjective human experience of sound and its interaction with activities, leading to an incomplete 'image' of users' auditory environments.
findings.quote: mainstream urban planning and design practice still largely rely on technologies that fall short of incorporating user knowledge and their activities

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Investigate potential correlations between contextual factors (e.g., amenities, weather, spatiotemporal aspects), user characteristics (e.g., demographics, familiarity, needs, expectations, purpose), user activities, and the physical and perceptual properties of their auditory environments.

Develop a metric to systematically assess the suitability for action of designed public spaces from an auditory perspective, identifying potential gaps between intended function and actual use of spaces.

Examine how different types of user activities (e.g., resting, socializing, active play) influence the perceived pleasantness and restorativeness of specific soundscapes, considering varying user characteristics.
bridge_warrants: The framework aims to integrate scientific knowledge (from acoustics, psychology, social sciences) with professional knowledge of planners and designers, and the experiential knowledge of users.
It bridges object-centered and human-centered approaches to sound by considering both physical measurements and perceptual descriptions of auditory environments.
It connects the study of urban form and activity patterns with the sensory dimension of public spaces, particularly sound.
methodological_critiques: Traditional ENM strategies are often unable or insufficient to reconcile knowledge from noise measurements with noise complaints from urban dwellers, as they rely on globally established indicators of sound levels that may not be relevant for local contexts and fail to capture the meanings of sounds or auditory comfort.

Current technologies used in mainstream urban planning and design practice fall short of incorporating user knowledge and their activities, providing an incomplete 'image' of users' auditory environments.

The definition of 'quiet areas' in European legislation is open to interpretation and lacks standardized methodology, making it difficult to implement in practice and relying on inaccurate assumptions about differentiating sound sources.
model_structure: The paper proposes an 'activity-centered framework' (Figure 1) with four main components: 'User' (defined by demographics, needs, familiarity, expectations, purpose), 'Activity' (a two-way link between User and Auditory Environments), 'Auditory Environments' (characterized by perceptual and acoustic sensor measurements), and 'Contextual Factors' (environmental conditions, spatiotemporal aspects, amenities). These components are interconnected through 'Theoretical and Applied Knowledge'.
limitations: Existing planning and design practices are primarily vision-oriented, neglecting other sensory dimensions like sound.
Sound is largely considered as a 'waste' (noise) to be managed, rather than a 'resource' to be designed for, in mainstream policy and practice.

Current technologies for acoustic data collection and analysis in practice often fail to integrate user-driven knowledge and activities, providing an incomplete understanding of auditory environments.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Considering Sound in Planning and Designing Public Spaces
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: We critically review the literature on the relationship between users of public spaces and their auditory environments, and how this knowledge is integrated in the planning, design, and management of public spaces as well as in technologies for acoustic and spatial data collection, analysis, and communication. To address the gaps identified in the review, we propose an activity-centered framework as a conceptual tool developed to support the integration of different types of knowledge in incorporating sound and the auditory environment in the planning and design of public spaces, by focusing on the activities that users perform in these spaces.
